title: How I Built a Side Project in 30 Days
briefDescription: A candid walkthrough of shipping something real from scratch — the planning, the pivots, and the lessons that actually stuck.
targets: Indie hackers, developers with side project ideas, anyone who keeps starting but never finishing.
body:
Week 1: The Idea Phase

The hardest part was just starting. I had a list of 12 ideas and spent the first three days paralysed by choice. Eventually I picked the one that scratched my own itch — a tool to track my reading across formats — and committed to it.

Week 2: Building Without Looking Up

I gave myself a rule: no tutorials, no YouTube rabbit holes. Just docs and the compiler errors. It slowed me down in the short term but I retained far more. By day 14 I had a working prototype.

Week 3: The Reality Check

I showed it to five people. Three were politely uninterested. One gave me a bug report I hadn't considered. One became my first real user. That ratio felt about right for a v0.1.

Week 4: Ship It

I deployed on a Friday night, wrote a short post, and went to sleep. Woke up to 40 sign-ups. Not viral by any measure, but proof that the idea had legs. The momentum from that pushed me through the next three months of iterations.

What I'd Do Differently

Talk to people earlier. Code is cheap to throw away; wasted assumptions are expensive. Next time I'm doing customer interviews before line one.

title: The Case for Boring Technology
briefDescription: Why choosing PostgreSQL, server-rendered HTML, and a monolith will serve most teams better than chasing the latest stack.
targets: Engineering leads, CTOs at early-stage companies, developers tired of framework fatigue.
body:
What Boring Means

Boring technology isn't old technology. It's technology whose failure modes are well understood, whose documentation is complete, and whose community has solved the edge cases you haven't hit yet.

The Hidden Cost of Novelty

Every new tool in your stack is a recruiting problem, an onboarding problem, and a debugging problem. When something breaks at 2am the last thing you want is to be the first person who's ever seen this error message.

PostgreSQL Does More Than You Think

Full-text search, JSON columns, pub/sub with LISTEN/NOTIFY, lateral joins, window functions. You probably don't need Elasticsearch, Redis, or a message queue. You need to read the Postgres docs more carefully.

When to Break the Rule

Boring technology has limits. If your problem is fundamentally about real-time at scale, or ML inference pipelines, you'll eventually outgrow the monolith. But most teams reach that point after they've hired 50 engineers, not before.

title: Understanding Async/Await from First Principles
briefDescription: A deep dive into what async/await actually compiles to, why the event loop matters, and how to avoid the most common mistakes.
targets: JavaScript developers who use async/await but aren't confident they truly understand it.
body:
What a Promise Actually Is

A Promise is an object that represents the eventual completion of an asynchronous operation. It has three states: pending, fulfilled, and rejected. The key insight is that a Promise doesn't make code run asynchronously — it just gives you a handle to a future value.

The Event Loop in 60 Seconds

JavaScript is single-threaded. The event loop is how it handles I/O without blocking. When you await something, you're yielding control back to the event loop until that operation resolves. Other code can run in the meantime.

The Waterfall Problem

The most common async/await mistake is sequential awaits when the operations are independent. const a = await fetchA(); const b = await fetchB(); runs them one after the other. const [a, b] = await Promise.all([fetchA(), fetchB()]); runs them in parallel.

Error Handling Patterns

try/catch works with async functions but has footguns. Unhandled promise rejections in event handlers won't be caught. Consider a utility wrapper that returns [error, result] tuples — it forces explicit error handling at each call site.

title: My Honest Review of Six Months Working Fully Remote
briefDescription: What actually changed, what I didn't expect, and the habits that made the difference between thriving and just surviving.
targets: People considering remote work, managers evaluating remote policies, anyone recently transitioning.
body:
Month 1: The Honeymoon

No commute. Music on. Coffee exactly how I like it. The first few weeks felt like a superpower unlock. I was shipping faster than I had in years and genuinely couldn't understand why everyone didn't work this way.

Month 2-3: The Friction

Loneliness crept in. Not dramatically — just the slow erosion of casual human contact. I noticed I was more irritable on days I didn't leave the house. The solution was embarrassingly simple: leave the house. Coworking space two days a week fixed it completely.

What Communication Looks Like Now

Everything requires more intentionality. You can't see when someone is deep in focus so you learn to batch your questions. Async-first culture sounds like a buzzword until you realise it means respecting people's attention the same way you'd want yours respected.

The Habits That Stuck

Morning walk before opening the laptop. Hard stop at 6pm. Weekly video call with at least three people just to see faces. These aren't productivity hacks — they're maintenance.

title: What I Learned Writing 100 Tests
briefDescription: Patterns, antipatterns, and the philosophical shift that made me actually enjoy writing tests instead of dreading them.
targets: Developers who write tests reluctantly, teams with flaky test suites, anyone trying to improve test culture.
body:
The Test That Changed My Mind

Test number 43 caught a bug I had no idea I'd introduced. It was a regression in a function I'd touched while fixing something else. Without the test, it would have shipped. With it, I found the bug in 30 seconds. That's when I stopped treating tests as a chore.

The Arrange-Act-Assert Pattern

Every test has three parts: set up the world, perform the action, verify the outcome. If your test is hard to read it's usually because these three parts are tangled. Separating them with blank lines or comments is not stylistic nitpicking — it's a legibility investment that pays off every time someone debugs a failure.

Antipattern: Testing Implementation Details

Tests that break every time you refactor are worse than no tests. Test what the function does, not how it does it. If your test imports internal functions that aren't exported, it's testing implementation.

The Test Pyramid Is Real

Many unit tests, fewer integration tests, very few E2E tests. Not because E2E tests aren't valuable — they are — but because they're slow, brittle, and expensive to maintain. Use them to cover the critical happy paths, not every edge case.

title: A Practical Guide to PostgreSQL Indexes
briefDescription: Everything you need to know about when to add an index, which type to use, and how to know if it's actually helping.
targets: Backend developers, anyone whose database queries are getting slow, engineers learning SQL performance.
body:
Why Indexes Exist

Without an index, Postgres scans every row in a table to find matches. With an index, it jumps directly to the matching rows. The tradeoff: indexes take up space and slow down writes because they must be maintained on every INSERT, UPDATE, and DELETE.

B-tree vs GIN vs GiST

B-tree is the default and handles equality and range queries. GIN (Generalized Inverted Index) is for full-text search and array containment. GiST handles geometric data and nearest-neighbor searches. For 95% of use cases, B-tree is what you want.

The EXPLAIN ANALYZE Command

Run EXPLAIN ANALYZE SELECT ... before and after adding an index. Look for "Seq Scan" turning into "Index Scan". Look at the actual time values — sometimes the query planner chooses a seq scan intentionally because the table is small enough that an index lookup is slower.

Composite Indexes and Column Order

A composite index on (user_id, created_at) helps queries filtering on both columns, and also queries filtering on just user_id. But it doesn't help queries filtering on just created_at. Leading columns matter — put the highest-cardinality, most-frequently-filtered column first.

title: How I Run My Freelance Practice Without Burning Out
briefDescription: Systems, boundaries, and the mindset shifts that took me from chaotic hustle to sustainable income over three years.
targets: Freelancers, consultants, developers considering going independent, anyone juggling too many clients.
body:
The Hourly Rate Trap

I started charging by the hour. Clients watched the clock. I felt guilty taking breaks. The incentive was to appear busy rather than be effective. Switching to project-based pricing changed everything — clients bought an outcome, I optimised for quality and speed.

The Two-Client Maximum

I never take more than two active clients at a time. Context-switching is expensive. Being fully present for two clients beats being half-present for four. I keep a waitlist and it has never cost me more revenue than it saved me in stress.

The Weekly Review Ritual

Every Friday at 4pm: review what shipped, update project trackers, draft the invoice, write three lines about what I'll do differently next week. Fifteen minutes. Keeps me from waking up Monday with no idea where anything stands.

Saying No Is a Skill

The best clients come from referrals from previous clients. The best referrals come from clients who thought working with you was effortless. The fastest way to earn that reputation is to under-promise and over-deliver, which means saying no to scope creep from day one.

title: TypeScript Generics: A Mental Model That Actually Works
briefDescription: Stop memorising syntax and start thinking about generics as variables for types — with worked examples from real codebases.
targets: TypeScript developers who feel shaky on generics, anyone who copy-pastes generic code without fully understanding it.
body:
Generics Are Type Variables

When you write function identity<T>(value: T): T, the T is a variable — just like a runtime variable, except it holds a type instead of a value. When you call identity(42), TypeScript infers T = number automatically.

Constraints Narrow the Possibilities

<T extends { id: number }> says: T can be any type, but it must have at least an id property of type number. Constraints let you write generic code that still has access to specific properties or methods.

The keyof Operator

function get<T, K extends keyof T>(obj: T, key: K): T[K] — this reads as: given an object of type T and a key that must be one of T's property names, return the value at that key. The return type T[K] is automatically the correct property type.

When Not to Use Generics

If you've written a generic and there's only one place it's called, it's not generic — it's just verbose. Generics earn their complexity when you're writing utility functions, data structures, or library code that must work across many different types.

title: The Reading System That Changed How I Learn
briefDescription: How I went from forgetting 90% of what I read to building a knowledge base I actually use — without any complicated apps.
targets: Knowledge workers, anyone who reads a lot but feels like it doesn't stick, lifelong learners.
body:
The Forgetting Curve Is Real

Without intervention, you forget roughly half of what you read within a day, and most of the rest within a week. This isn't a personal failing — it's neuroscience. The question is what interventions actually work.

The Only Highlighting Rule I Follow

I only highlight something if I would be embarrassed not to remember it in a year. This constraint dramatically reduces how much I highlight. A page with no highlights is fine. A page with 12 highlights means I didn't apply the rule.

The Two-Page Summary Habit

After finishing a book, I write a two-page summary from memory. No looking at highlights first. The act of retrieval is more effective for retention than any amount of re-reading. Then I check my summary against my highlights and note the gaps.

The 30-Day Review

Thirty days after finishing a book, I re-read just my two-page summary. This single review, at the right spacing, does more for long-term retention than a dozen re-reads in the first week. After that, I add it to my annual review pile.

title: Designing REST APIs That Don't Annoy Developers
briefDescription: A collection of principles I've assembled from building and consuming hundreds of APIs — the decisions that make or break developer experience.
targets: Backend developers, API designers, anyone building a product with a public or internal API.
body:
Use Nouns, Not Verbs

/api/get-user is an anti-pattern. /api/users/:id is correct. The HTTP method (GET, POST, PATCH, DELETE) is the verb. The path is the resource. Mixing both creates ambiguity and breaks expectations.

Be Consistent With Status Codes

200 for success. 201 for created resources. 400 for client errors (bad input). 401 for authentication required. 403 for authorisation denied (authenticated but not permitted). 404 for not found. 422 for validation errors. 500 for server errors. Pick a convention and never deviate.

Error Responses Need a Body

A 400 with an empty body is useless. A 400 with {"message": "email must be a valid email address"} saves the developer 20 minutes of guessing. Error bodies should be machine-readable (consistent structure) and human-readable (plain English message).

Version From Day One

Even if you think you'll never need it, put /api/v1/ in your URL now. When you inevitably need to make breaking changes, you'll have a migration path. Changing /api/users to /api/v2/users after clients depend on it is painful.

title: Notes from Six Years of Daily Journaling
briefDescription: What I've learned about memory, clarity, and pattern recognition from six years of writing every morning — and why I'll never stop.
targets: Anyone curious about journaling, people who've tried and quit, writers who want to develop a daily practice.
body:
Year One: The Wrong Reasons

I started journaling because a book told me it would make me more productive. I was doing it for the outcome, not the process. I quit after three months because I couldn't measure the productivity gains. I started again two years later because I wanted to remember things more clearly. That framing stuck.

What Actually Goes In It

Decisions and the reasoning behind them. Things I want to remember about a conversation. Questions I don't have answers to. Observations about patterns in my own behaviour. Gratitude when I feel it. Frustrations I need to process before I can move on. Not diary entries — more like a running conversation with myself.

The Rereading Habit

Every year on January 1st I read the previous year's journal. The experience is humbling. Problems I was certain would derail me are barely mentioned by June. Opportunities I dismissed turned out to be significant. Rereading is where the compound interest actually accumulates.

The Format Doesn't Matter

Paper, app, text file — it doesn't matter. What matters is that you can write quickly, revisit easily, and feel no friction. I've used three different tools over six years. The consistency was in the habit, not the tool.

title: Kubernetes for People Who Don't Want to Learn Kubernetes
briefDescription: The minimum viable understanding of Kubernetes that will let you ship containerised applications without becoming a platform engineer.
targets: Backend developers forced to use Kubernetes, engineers moving from traditional hosting to containers.
body:
What Kubernetes Actually Does

Kubernetes is a container orchestrator. It runs your Docker containers, restarts them when they crash, distributes traffic across multiple instances, and handles rolling deployments without downtime. You describe the desired state in YAML, Kubernetes makes reality match that description.

The Three Concepts You Can't Skip

A Pod is the smallest deployable unit — one or more containers that run together. A Deployment declares how many replicas of a pod you want and handles rolling updates. A Service is a stable network endpoint that routes traffic to your pods regardless of which specific pod is handling requests.

The YAML You'll Write 80% of the Time

Deployments and Services. The Deployment says "run 3 replicas of image X, inject these env vars, give each 256MB of RAM". The Service says "expose port 3000 on all matching pods". Everything else — Ingress, ConfigMaps, Secrets — builds on top of these two.

What Not to Manage Yourself

Use a managed Kubernetes service (EKS, GKE, AKS). Manage your own etcd cluster only if you have a platform team whose job is Kubernetes. For everyone else: pay the cloud tax and spend the saved time building your product.

title: The First 90 Days at a New Engineering Job
briefDescription: What to prioritise, what to avoid, and how to build the kind of credibility that compounds over a career.
targets: Developers starting a new job, engineering managers helping new hires, anyone who wants to onboard more effectively.
body:
Listen More Than You Talk

The instinct to prove yourself quickly leads to bad outcomes. Before you can improve anything you need to understand why it is the way it is. Most things that look broken have a reason behind them — asking about that reason is how you learn the context that makes your eventual suggestions actually useful.

Ship Something Small in the First Two Weeks

Find the smallest meaningful thing you can complete and ship it. Not to prove yourself — to understand the deployment process, the review culture, the testing requirements. Small, real contributions teach you more about how a team works than any amount of documentation reading.

Build Your Debugging Map

Where do the logs live? Who knows which subsystem? What does on-call look like? Where are the runbooks? This information is priceless at 2am and nearly impossible to document comprehensively. Acquire it through conversations and note it somewhere personal.

The Reputation That Matters

Reliability compounds. The engineer who consistently closes things they pick up, communicates blockers early, and delivers without drama builds a reputation that opens doors for years. Technical skills are table stakes. Trustworthiness is rare.

title: Why I Deleted Social Media and What Replaced It
briefDescription: Three years after deleting my accounts: what I gained, what I missed, and what the experience taught me about attention.
targets: Anyone considering a digital detox, people feeling overwhelmed by social media, curious observers.
body:
The Reason I Actually Did It

I tracked my screen time for one week. Eleven hours on Twitter. That's not a statistic — that's a quarter of my waking hours. I couldn't remember what I had done with those hours. I couldn't point to a single thing that was better because I'd spent them there.

The First Month Was Uncomfortable

The phantom urge to open the app. The vague anxiety that I was missing something. The realisation that I had been using the feed as a way to avoid thinking. These feelings faded. What replaced them was uncomfortable in a different way: I had to decide what to do with my attention rather than having it decided for me.

What I Actually Missed

Local community events I used to find via Facebook groups. Occasional genuinely useful industry conversations. The ability to quickly look someone up. These were real losses. I solved two of them with RSS feeds and newsletters. The third I mostly didn't need.

The Net Result

I read more. I write more. I have longer conversations. I remember more of what I read. I am not claiming this is for everyone — but the decision was the right one for me, and I made it by looking honestly at the data rather than the theory.

title: Container Security Fundamentals You Can't Skip
briefDescription: The security decisions that matter most when running containers in production — practical, actionable, and ruthlessly prioritised.
targets: DevOps engineers, backend developers deploying containers, teams moving to cloud-native infrastructure.
body:
Never Run as Root

By default, Docker containers run as root inside the container. If an attacker escapes the container, they have root on the host. Add USER nonroot to your Dockerfile. It takes 30 seconds and removes a major attack surface.

Use Read-Only Filesystems

Most application containers don't need to write to the filesystem. --read-only flag (or readOnlyRootFilesystem: true in Kubernetes) means an attacker who compromises your container can't drop files, install tools, or persist malware.

Scan Your Images

Run docker scout cves or Trivy in your CI pipeline. Most CVEs in production containers come from the base image, not your application code. Updating FROM node:20-alpine to the latest patch regularly eliminates the vast majority of known vulnerabilities.

Secrets Are Not Environment Variables

Environment variables are visible in docker inspect, process listings, and crash dumps. Use a secrets manager (AWS Secrets Manager, Vault, Kubernetes Secrets with encryption at rest) and mount secrets as files, not env vars.

title: Learning to Say No: A Developer's Guide to Scope Management
briefDescription: Practical scripts, frameworks, and mindset shifts for pushing back on unreasonable requests without damaging relationships.
targets: Developers overwhelmed by feature requests, anyone who struggles to set boundaries at work.
body:
The Cost of Yes

Every yes is a no to something else. When you say yes to the third urgent feature this week, you're saying no to the code review you've been promising, the refactor that will make the codebase maintainable, and the focused time that produces your best work. Making the trade-off explicit helps you evaluate it honestly.

"Yes, And" vs "Yes"

"I can do that" is a complete sentence that commits you fully. "I can do that — it would push the API work to next sprint, is that okay?" is the same thing with the trade-off surfaced. Most of the time, the requester doesn't know they're asking you to sacrifice something else. Showing them the trade-off changes the conversation.

The Written List

Keep a public, shared list of everything you're working on. When someone asks for something new, you can point to the list and ask where this fits. The list does the saying-no for you — it's not your opinion, it's the physics of time.

Protecting Deep Work

Block 3-hour windows in your calendar for focused work. Treat them like meetings you can't cancel. When someone requests that time, you're not saying no to them — you're saying the time is already committed. Which it is.

title: The Architecture of a Production-Ready Node.js Application
briefDescription: The patterns, tooling, and structural decisions that separate a weekend project from software that can actually be maintained and scaled.
targets: Node.js developers moving beyond tutorials, teams evaluating their app structure, anyone building their second or third serious project.
body:
Separate Configuration from Code

Configuration is anything that changes between environments: database URLs, API keys, feature flags. It should never be hardcoded. Use environment variables and validate them at startup — fail fast with a clear error rather than failing silently at runtime when the missing config is actually accessed.

The Controller-Service-Repository Pattern

Controllers handle HTTP: parse the request, call a service, format the response. Services contain business logic: validation, orchestration, rules. Repositories handle data access: SQL queries, cache reads, external API calls. This separation makes each layer testable in isolation and replaceable without affecting the others.

Structured Logging From Day One

JSON logs are queryable. String logs are not. Every log entry should have at minimum: timestamp, level, message, and a request ID that links all log entries from a single request together. Adding this after the fact, across a large codebase, is painful.

Graceful Shutdown

Handle SIGTERM. Stop accepting new connections. Wait for in-flight requests to complete. Close database connections cleanly. This matters because Kubernetes sends SIGTERM before killing a container — applications that don't handle it correctly drop requests during deployments.

title: What Three Years of Meditation Actually Changed
briefDescription: An honest, non-mystical account of what a daily practice has and hasn't changed — with specific examples.
targets: Skeptics curious about meditation, people who've tried and found it useless, pragmatic seekers.
body:
Why I Started

Not for enlightenment. I was reactive — quick to frustration, slow to recover from setbacks. Someone I respected suggested a 10-minute daily practice. I committed to 30 days to have an honest basis for evaluation.

What Changed After 30 Days

Almost nothing perceptible. The practice felt mechanical and I couldn't tell if I was doing it correctly. What I did notice was a very slight increase in the gap between stimulus and reaction in high-stress situations. Small but real.

What Changed After Three Years

I recover from frustration faster. I notice when I'm catastrophising before I've fully spiralled. I'm less uncomfortable with silence. I sleep better. None of these are mystical claims — they're observable changes in behaviour that other people have noticed and commented on without knowing I meditate.

What Didn't Change

I'm still impatient. I still have bad days. I still get anxious before important events. Meditation isn't a cure — it's maintenance. Like exercise, the effects accumulate and diminish in roughly equal proportion to the consistency of the practice.

title: Git Workflows That Scale With Your Team
briefDescription: A practical comparison of trunk-based development, Gitflow, and GitHub Flow — with advice on choosing based on your actual constraints.
targets: Engineering teams evaluating their branching strategy, developers frustrated with their current workflow, team leads.
body:
The Problem With Gitflow in 2025

Gitflow was designed for scheduled, versioned releases. Most teams today deploy continuously. Maintaining multiple long-lived branches (main, develop, release/*, hotfix/*) creates merge overhead and divergence that compounds over time. If you deploy every day, Gitflow is solving a problem you don't have.

Trunk-Based Development: The Case For

One branch. Short-lived feature branches (hours, not days). Merge into main frequently. Feature flags for incomplete work. This is how Google, Meta, and most high-velocity teams operate. The requirement is a strong CI pipeline — you must be confident that merging to main won't break production.

GitHub Flow: The Sensible Middle Ground

Feature branches + pull requests + merge to main + deploy. No develop branch. No release branches. Works well for teams of 2-20 with a basic CI setup. The conventions are minimal enough that everyone can follow them.

The Real Differentiator Is CI

The branching strategy you can use is determined by the quality of your automated testing. Teams with excellent test coverage can merge to main multiple times a day safely. Teams without it need longer-lived branches to act as a buffer. Investment in testing is investment in workflow flexibility.

title: How I Improved My Writing by Reading It Aloud
briefDescription: A deceptively simple technique that surfaces every awkward sentence, unnecessary word, and unclear idea before anyone else reads it.
targets: Technical writers, bloggers, anyone whose written communication is part of their job.
body:
The Technique

Write your draft. Wait a few hours. Read it aloud in a room alone. Every time you stumble, hesitate, or have to re-read a sentence to understand it — that's a problem. Mark it. Revise it. Repeat until you can read the whole piece without pausing.

Why It Works

Written prose that we read silently gets processed differently than prose we hear. We fill in gaps, make charitable inferences, and speed past awkward constructions. Hearing the words out loud bypasses these shortcuts. The brain processes it more like conversation — and conversation has a very low tolerance for ambiguity.

What It Catches

Run-on sentences that felt fine on the screen. Repeated words in adjacent sentences. Transitions that don't connect what they're supposed to connect. Jargon that I'd normalised but a reader hadn't. Sentences that require two reads to parse.

The Side Effect

I started writing shorter sentences. Not because I was told to — because when I read long sentences aloud I ran out of breath or lost the thread before reaching the verb. The constraint created the clarity.

title: Database Migrations Without the 3am Incident
briefDescription: The practices that make database migrations boring and reversible instead of terrifying and irreversible.
targets: Backend developers running migrations on production databases, teams that have been burned by bad migrations.
body:
The Golden Rule: Never Lock a Large Table

Adding a NOT NULL column to a 50-million-row table locks the table for the duration of the backfill. On a busy database, that's a production incident. Add the column as nullable, deploy, backfill in batches outside a transaction, then add the NOT NULL constraint once the backfill is complete.

Additive Changes First

Deploy database changes before application code changes. Add the new column with a default. Deploy the code that reads from both old and new columns. Then run the migration. Then deploy the code that only reads the new column. Then drop the old column. This sequence means you can rollback the application code at any step without a database rollback.

Every Migration Needs a Down Script

If your migration tool has up/down steps, write both. Even if you never run the down migration — the exercise of writing it forces you to think about whether the migration is reversible. If you can't write a down migration, you're probably doing something dangerous.

Test Your Migration on a Prod Clone

Run it on a database of the same size, with the same indexes and data distribution. A migration that takes 0.1 seconds on a 1,000-row dev table might take 4 hours on a 500-million-row prod table. You want to know this before not after.

title: The Tools That Actually Survived My Productivity Stack Purge
briefDescription: After years of chasing the perfect system, I cut everything down to four tools. Here's what survived and why.
targets: Productivity tool junkies, developers overwhelmed by their own systems, people looking to simplify.
body:
The Purge

I counted once: 14 active productivity tools. Task managers, note-takers, time trackers, habit trackers, calendar apps, focus timers. The overhead of maintaining the system was competing with the actual work. I spent a weekend deciding what to keep based on one question: does this solve a problem I actually have, or a problem I'm afraid I might have?

The Calendar

Non-negotiable. Time is finite and shared. Everything that requires a specific time goes here. I've tried integrating tasks and notes into the calendar — it doesn't work. The calendar is for time, not content.

The Text Editor

For everything that isn't a specific time. Notes, drafts, quick captures, meeting notes, thinking. Plain text files, synced across devices. No formatting, no tags, no hierarchy. Full-text search is the filing system.

The Task List

One list. Not projects, not areas, not someday/maybe. One flat list of things I'm actually going to do this week. Everything else lives in the text editor as a reference, not a task. The list is reviewed every Monday and Friday. That's it.

title: React Performance: The Problems Worth Solving
briefDescription: Which React performance issues actually matter, how to measure before you optimise, and the fixes that give the biggest bang for the byte.
targets: React developers seeing slow renders, frontend engineers who've heard about memo and useCallback but aren't sure when to reach for them.
body:
Measure Before You Optimise

The React DevTools Profiler tells you exactly which components rendered, how long each render took, and what triggered the render. Open it before writing a single line of optimisation code. Half the time, the slow component isn't where you thought it was.

When memo Actually Helps

React.memo prevents a component from re-rendering when its parent re-renders, provided its props haven't changed. It only helps if the parent renders frequently AND the component is expensive to render. Wrapping every component in memo adds reference comparison overhead without benefit.

The useCallback Trap

Every function defined inline in a component is recreated on every render. Wrapping it in useCallback only helps if that function is passed as a prop to a memoised component. Standalone useCallback — without memo on the child — does nothing useful.

The Biggest Win: Virtualise Long Lists

Rendering 1,000 rows to the DOM is expensive regardless of React. Use react-window or react-virtual to only render the rows in the viewport. This often produces a 10x improvement in scroll performance that no amount of memo/useCallback tuning can match.

title: What Burnout Actually Feels Like (And the Slow Recovery)
briefDescription: A personal account of hitting the wall after four years of high-output work — what the warning signs were, and what actually helped.
targets: Developers pushing hard, anyone who suspects they might be burning out, managers watching for signs in their teams.
body:
The Warning Signs I Ignored

Irritability at things that wouldn't normally bother me. Difficulty concentrating on anything longer than 15 minutes. Opening the laptop and sitting there unable to start. These weren't dramatic — they crept up slowly over months. I kept attributing them to being tired, to the season, to external events. I was wrong.

What It Actually Was

Not a deficit of motivation — a depletion of capacity. The difference matters. Motivation techniques (Pomodoro timers, goal setting, accountability partners) don't fix depletion. They can actually make it worse by treating a rest problem as a discipline problem.

What Helped

Three weeks completely off. Not "off but checking Slack" — actually off. Then a return to work at 60% capacity for two months. Then a slow rebuild. The recovery was longer and slower than I wanted it to be. It took exactly as long as it needed to.

The Structural Change

I now treat sustained high output the way an athlete treats training load: increase gradually, with planned recovery built in. The goal isn't to work as hard as possible — it's to work at a level that's sustainable for years, not quarters.

title: CI/CD Pipelines That Actually Help Your Team
briefDescription: The pipeline setup that reduces toil, catches real bugs, and stays fast enough that engineers don't route around it.
targets: Engineers setting up CI/CD, teams with slow or flaky pipelines, anyone who treats CI as a checkbox.
body:
Speed Is a Feature

A CI pipeline that takes 45 minutes will be bypassed. Engineers will push straight to main, disable checks, or deploy manually. A pipeline that takes 5 minutes will be used as intended. Speed isn't a nice-to-have — it's the difference between a pipeline that improves quality and one that just creates the appearance of quality.

The Pipeline Tiers

Fast checks (lint, type-check, unit tests) run on every push — under 3 minutes. Slower checks (integration tests, E2E on critical paths) run on PRs — under 10 minutes. Full E2E and load tests run on merges to main — can be longer. Keeping these tiers separate lets engineers get fast feedback during development.

Flaky Tests Are Worse Than No Tests

A test that sometimes passes and sometimes fails trains engineers to ignore failures. Every flaky test must be fixed or deleted immediately. Zero tolerance is not perfectionism — it's protecting the signal value of the pipeline.

Cache Aggressively

Caching node_modules, Docker layers, and build artifacts can cut pipeline time in half. Most CI platforms support this natively. Set it up once, re-evaluate the cache keys quarterly, and you'll spend almost no time on it thereafter.

title: The Hiring Process I Actually Believe In
briefDescription: What I changed after realising our process was optimising for confidence over competence — and the results three years later.
targets: Engineering managers, team leads involved in hiring, anyone who's been through a broken interview process.
body:
What We Were Optimising For

The standard whiteboard interview measures whether a candidate can solve algorithmic puzzles under pressure while being watched by strangers. The job requires building software collaboratively over weeks while consulting documentation, Stack Overflow, and colleagues freely. The correlation between these two skills is weak.

The Work Sample Approach

We replaced the whiteboard with a small, realistic project similar to our actual work. Candidates have a week to complete it at home, using any tools they'd normally use. We evaluate the result, then do a 30-minute code review conversation about their decisions. We see real work and get a preview of what code review conversations with them will look like.

What We Look For In Review

How do they handle disagreement? Do they understand the trade-offs behind their decisions, or were they just copying a pattern? Can they articulate why they chose one approach over another? How do they respond when I suggest a different approach? These qualities matter far more than whether they nailed a binary tree reversal.

The Results

Lower attrition in the first year. Faster ramp-up. More diverse candidates making it through. Candidates who have worked with us consistently say the process was the most respectful hiring experience they'd had.

title: Monitoring Production Without Going Mad
briefDescription: The alert philosophy, dashboard design, and on-call practices that produce genuine signal instead of alert fatigue.
targets: Engineers setting up monitoring, teams drowning in alerts, anyone designing an on-call rotation.
body:
The Alert Fatigue Problem

Every alert that fires and requires no action trains engineers to treat alerts as background noise. Within months of a noisy system going live, the median response to an alert is a glance and a dismiss. The monitor that cried wolf.

Page on Symptoms, Not Causes

Don't alert when CPU is above 80%. Alert when response time p99 is above your SLA threshold. CPU might be high for completely harmless reasons. Response time being slow always means users are experiencing something bad. Symptom-based alerting has a dramatically lower false-positive rate.

The On-Call Rulebook

Every alert that wakes someone up must have a runbook. The runbook must have been written by someone other than the engineer who wrote the alert. If an alert fires twice with no action required, it must be either fixed or deleted before the next on-call rotation starts.

The Dashboard That Gets Used

One page. The four numbers that tell you if the service is healthy: error rate, request rate, p99 latency, and queue depth (if applicable). Everything else is a drill-down for investigation. A dashboard with 40 panels that nobody looks at is not a dashboard — it's an alibi.

title: Why I Became a Technical Writer (And Why More Engineers Should)
briefDescription: The career path I stumbled into and why the skills involved — clarity, empathy, structure — are the most underrated in engineering.
targets: Engineers curious about adjacent roles, developers who enjoy writing, anyone thinking about career pivots.
body:
How It Happened

I was the developer who kept volunteering to write the documentation because I found it interesting. After two years I was spending more time on it than on code. Someone suggested I should get paid for the thing I was already doing. The conversation that followed changed my career trajectory.

What Technical Writing Actually Is

Understanding complex systems deeply enough to explain them clearly to someone who doesn't share your context. The engineering background helps — you can read the source code, ask the right questions, and recognise when an explanation is incomplete. But the core skill is empathy: imagining what the reader knows and doesn't know.

The Skills That Transferred

Debugging. When documentation is wrong, you trace the inconsistency to its source the same way you trace a bug. Systematic thinking. A docs site is an information architecture problem. User focus. The reader is the user; the test is whether they can accomplish their goal.

Why Engineers Should Try It

You cannot write a clear explanation of something you don't fully understand. Forcing yourself to document a system reveals gaps in your own understanding. Every engineer who has written documentation reports understanding the system better afterward than before.

title: What I Got Wrong About Startups in My 20s
briefDescription: The beliefs that cost me time, money, and energy — and the reframes that eventually replaced them.
targets: Early-career developers at startups, founders, people seduced by startup mythology.
body:
The Hustle Fallacy

I believed that working more hours than everyone else was a competitive advantage. It is — for about six months. After that, the sleep debt, the narrowed focus, and the interpersonal friction created by exhaustion erased most of the output gains. The people I most admired were working hard but also resting hard.

The Wrong Kind of Fast

Speed that accumulates technical debt is speed that borrows against the future. I shipped things quickly by skipping tests, ignoring edge cases, and making architecture decisions I knew were wrong. The compound interest on those decisions made years 2-4 significantly harder than they needed to be.

The Equity Myth

I took lower salaries at two companies in exchange for equity that was worth nothing by the time I could exercise it. The lesson wasn't that equity is always worthless — it's that you should understand the capitalisation table, the preference stack, and the realistic liquidation scenarios before accepting below-market cash.

The Real Value of Startups

Speed of learning. Scope of responsibility. Access to problems you wouldn't touch for years at a large company. These things are genuinely valuable and not everywhere. I don't regret any of it — I just wish I'd been less naive about the specific trade-offs I was making.
